name: Aruba
summary: Aruba has no forced heirship since its new inheritance law took effect on 1 September 2021, so a will can leave the estate to anyone. Children can still claim a capped lump sum, and a surviving spouse has statutory rights. Aruba has no trust law and the Hague Trusts Convention is not extended to it; a private foundation is not available in the full form found in Curaçao.
family_claims: Book 4 gives a child a lump-sum claim against the heirs for care and upbringing (to age 18), living and study costs (to 21, extendable to 25) and unpaid work in the parent's household or business. The lump sum cannot exceed half the estate. The surviving spouse has statutory rights (legal division, usufruct of the home).
foreign_law_note: No source read states Aruba's conflict rule for the estate of a foreign national, or whether a foreigner may choose the law of their nationality.
trust_note: The HCCH table shows the Netherlands' extension covering Curaçao only; Aruba is not listed, so the Convention is not in force there. No Aruban trust statute was found. Foundations (stichting) sit in Book 2 of the Civil Code, in force 1 January 2021; a 2019 commentary says a private foundation was considered and dismissed, so only ordinary foundations exist.
open_questions: Aruba's private international law rule for succession of foreign nationals was not sourced.
Transition rules for estates opened before 1 September 2021 were not read.
The text of Aruba's Book 4 was not read; the rules above come from a law-firm summary.
Whether Aruba has any trust statute or a private foundation form was not confirmed against Book 2 itself.
